newsitem.title: FRANCE: Protesters mourn before French far-right rally.
newsitem.headline: Protesters mourn before French far-right rally.

text.p: Black flowers and the French motto "liberty, equality, fraternity" sprouted across Strasbourg hours before a congress of the far-right National Front on Saturday which officials fear may spark clashes.
Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, a vituperative orator who backs sending even legal immigrants home, has vowed an assault on the political establishment in the run-up to a March 1998 general election.

Security forces ringed off the conference centre which will host the meeting as protestors preparing a counter-demonstration decorated the Alsatian capital with symbols of opposition to the anti-immigration party.

Black flowers were planted outside the European Parliament "to mourn the death of democracy", a black flag was briefly hoisted on the spire of the towering Gothic cathedral, and black bands wrapped around street signs.

The Socialist city hall put up posters carrying the Republican slogan in myriad languages. A few hundred protestors carrying cardboard suitcases crossed the Rhine river away from the city to show their discontent.
Tens of thousands of people are expected to take part in an anti-Front demonstration on Saturday afternoon.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin and Communist chief Robert Hue, in interviews published by the daily Le Parisien on Saturday, denounced the Front as racist, xenophobic, anti-Semitic, and fascist.

"Contrary to what one government representative said in appealing for 'respect of all opinions', we mustn't respect the ideas of the extreme-right, we have to fight them. Racism and anti-Semitism are not 'opinions' but offences," Jospin said.
Jospin, Hue and Greens leader Dominique Voynet will be among the marchers on Saturday. Police reinforcements have been called in by Strasbourg mayor Catherine Trautmann.

Trautmann said she hoped the demonstration would counter the Front's resurgence -- one in four Alsatian voters backed it in the 1995 presidential poll -- and "would take place in a calm and dignified fashion".
Though advised to ban the congress on grounds it threatened public order, Trautmann let it go forward although she planned to lead Saturday's protest march.
Countering the Front's presence has divided Strasbourg, with parties of the centre-right coalition ruling France refusing to participate in the demonstration.

"Racism can be likened to terrorism. We fight together against terrorism, but we are divided against racism. That is unacceptable," said Jean Kahn, former president of the CRIF, umbrella body for French Jewish associations.
President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist Rally for the Republic said the protests played into Le Pen's hands. "These demonstrations are a major error," said its secretary-general Jean-Francois Mancel.

The Front "knows it cannot win the election on its own. But it would score a great victory if the conservatives lost and the Socialist Party returned to power. So it will portray itself as the only hope of the Right against the Left," he said.
The two-round, first-past-the-post polling system has kept the Front out of parliament, and an Ipsos survey published on Friday said it would remain out if the election were held now.
But political analysts believe the Front could end up on the second ballot, potentially holding the balance of power, in 150 to 220 of France's 577 constituencies.
